title: Risk E. Rat's Pizza and Amusement Center

jokes.text: The gang nostalgically sings along to the Risk E. Rat's jingle in the car, completely unironically, as grown adults.
jokes.setup: The episode opens with a cheesy children's pizza place jingle playing in the car.
jokes.punchline: The gang — grown adult men — are singing along with genuine enthusiasm and emotional investment in a children's restaurant.
jokes.explanation: A solid cold open gag — the joke is entirely in the disconnect between the childish jingle and the adult men's sincere enthusiasm. Sets up the episode's premise efficiently. Character-appropriate but not especially novel for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like, that's where I became a man and saw my first set of boobies, at Risk E.'s.

jokes.text: "That's where I became a man and saw my first set of boobies, at Risk E.'s."
jokes.setup: The gang is enthusiastically recalling what made Risk E. Rat's special — arcade games, pizza, comedy.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's formative childhood memory at a kids' pizza place is seeing an animatronic robot's breasts backstage.
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — Charlie's warped, naïve sexuality is perfectly expressed in this reveal. The specificity of 'animatronic robot' makes it weird and funny rather than just crude. The 'since my mom's' capper elevates it significantly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Justine the Teen Dream. She was one of the robots in the Animatronic No Rules Band.

jokes.text: "That was the fir-first set of boobs I ever saw since my mom's, so..."
jokes.setup: Charlie has just revealed he saw animatronic breasts as his sexual awakening.
jokes.punchline: He casually clarifies 'since my mom's' — implying he saw his mother's breasts first, delivered with zero self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The 'since my mom's' capper lands as a delayed detonation — you're already laughing at the animatronic line, then Charlie adds this with total nonchalance. It's perfectly in character (Charlie's deeply disturbed home life is a series-long thread), it's economical (just four words), and the casual trailing 'so...' makes it even funnier. This is what great dark comedy looks like — the horror is in the normalcy of delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That was the fir-first set of boobs I ever saw since my mom's, so...

jokes.text: "So if you got off the Train to Kid City and you snuck backstage, you could see under her shirt just before she came out to perform."
jokes.setup: Charlie is explaining the logistics of how to peep at animatronic breasts at a children's restaurant.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate ritual — specific train name, sneaking backstage, timing the peek — makes this worse by implying this was a well-known, repeated practice.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Train to Kid City' is good world-building, and Mac and Dennis's knowing 'uh-huh' reactions confirm this was common knowledge. Sustains the creepiness of the opening joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Then you learned your lesson, and they'd send you back out to unleash it on the kids.

jokes.text: Mac's concern about missing out on childhood, specifically the animatronic boobs.
jokes.setup: Mac says he can't get past 'this whole Justine the Teen Dream thing' and feeling like he 'missed out on his childhood.'
jokes.punchline: His sense of lost childhood is specifically pegged to not having seen an animatronic robot's breasts — which he's sad about as an adult.
jokes.explanation: Good character work — Mac's particular brand of stunted masculinity and obsession with proving his heterosexuality makes this specific grievance fitting. The 'yes, I do' / 'yeah, let's go' exchange with Charlie is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, I agree it's total bullshit that we would have to sign a waiver and also that we could bum-rush you and there's nothing you could do about it.

jokes.text: "Well, they're gonna go check out some animatronic titties, so..."
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have just wordlessly agreed to go sneak backstage to look at the animatronic robot.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a completely deadpan summary of what they're doing to Frank, as if it's a totally normal errand.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's flat delivery of 'animatronic titties' is funny precisely because of how normal he makes it sound. Classic Dennis straight-man-to-the-chaos role, though he's also complicit.

dialogue.line: Frank drinking water from the fountain like an animal

jokes.text: The soundproofed bar for moms — 'they would get hammered' while kids ran wild
jokes.setup: Gang notices the place has been spruced up
jokes.punchline: They fondly recall the soundproofed mom bar where parents would get blackout drunk to survive the noise
jokes.explanation: Decent nostalgic dark joke about childhood chaos. Relatable observation about Chuck E. Cheese-type venues but doesn't push into real Sunny darkness. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Where he would smack his kids in the head because they were pieces of shit and then he would bust his brother because he was a lazy drunk.

jokes.text: "You would just go and sit there and fester in your candy-fueled rage for about 20 minutes. Then you learned your lesson, and they'd send you back out to unleash it on the kids."
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining what the Time-Out Room was actually for.
jokes.punchline: The 'lesson' of the time-out room was simply to let the rage ferment and then release a more concentrated version of it back onto the other children.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'candy-fueled rage' is a great piece of writing — specific, visual, and captures something true about children's behavior at these places. The logic that you're 'unleashing' the rage back is a nice absurdist inversion of what discipline is supposed to do.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, because of their race.

jokes.text: Frank is spotted drinking water from the fountain in what is clearly an odd, aggressive, or eccentric manner that makes the staff yell at him.
jokes.setup: The gang has just signed waivers to get in. Frank has gone quiet.
jokes.punchline: Staff member: 'What the hell are you doing?' Frank: 'Drinking water. What does it look like I'm doing?' — implying he's doing it in some bizarre, inappropriate way.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank visual gag — the joke lives entirely in the visual of how he's drinking water that we don't see. His perfectly innocent 'what does it look like I'm doing?' is very Frank. The rewatch_bonus is high because seeing the visual is funnier than inferring it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: How do I simulate real-world violence with something like that?

jokes.text: Frank attempts to tip the teenager by loudly calling him by the wrong name, then the teen says 'That's not my name'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to be magnanimous and tip the waiver kid
jokes.punchline: He calls him by a dismissive wrong name as though that's normal, and the kid's flat correction is the entire punchline
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank dismissiveness toward low-status workers. The kid's flat 'That's not my name' is the best part. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: To get it out of my system, bozo.

jokes.text: "Where are your guns? ... I'm very specifically looking for Risk E.'s rifle. It had a real heavy feel to it, it was very realistic, had a good smoky bang."
jokes.setup: Frank approaches the prize counter looking to redeem his old tickets.
jokes.punchline: Instead of normal prizes, Frank demands a realistic rifle toy — and his description ('very realistic,' 'good smoky bang,' firing pebbles at Charlie's eye) makes clear he used it as an actual weapon.
jokes.explanation: Frank's characterization as a man who weaponized children's toys is excellent. 'I could fire them right at Charlie's eye. It was awesome.' — this is both a character joke and a commentary on how dangerous toys used to be. The escalating specificity works well.

dialogue.speaker: Employee
dialogue.line: Those were discontinued because cigarettes are illegal.

jokes.text: Frank wants to redeem his 'old tickets' at the prize counter — implying he has held onto tickets from childhood
jokes.setup: Frank announces his plan for the visit
jokes.punchline: He's been holding tickets from childhood decades ago and plans to cash them in now — the mundane delivery makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Good Frank detail — the implication that he's kept these tickets for 40+ years is very on-brand. Pays off later when we see what he wants to redeem them for.

dialogue.line: That's what the bone's for! That's what the bone was for!

jokes.text: "What the hell am I supposed to do with an orange space laser? Have you ever seen anybody use a space laser in real life? How do I simulate real-world violence with something like that?"
jokes.setup: The prize counter employee offers Frank an 'orange space laser' as a substitute for the realistic rifle.
jokes.punchline: Frank's objection is entirely practical — the problem with the space laser is that it can't simulate real-world violence, which Frank treats as a self-evident purpose of toy prizes.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Frank lines. The logic is impeccable from Frank's perspective — a toy should prepare you for real violence, and a space laser fails that test. 'How do I simulate real-world violence with something like that?' is a quotable line because it's delivered as a completely sincere grievance. The employee's baffled 'why would you want to simulate real-world violence?' gets the perfect straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And it's also good for the girls because then they know what they're supposed to look like.

jokes.text: "To get it out of my system, bozo."
jokes.setup: Employee asks why anyone would want to simulate real-world violence.
jokes.punchline: Frank's answer is delivered as if it's the most obvious thing in the world.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Five words that capture Frank's entire worldview. The 'bozo' is an excellent touch — Frank calling the employee a clown for not understanding why toy violence is cathartic is a great inversion.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: These balls have no weight to 'em. Back in my day, you could crush a man's skull with one of these.

jokes.text: Frank's escalating list of discontinued items: switchblades-that-are-combs, tobacco-flavored gum for fake dip, candy cigarettes.
jokes.setup: Frank can't get the rifle, so he pivots to other nostalgic prizes.
jokes.punchline: Each successive item is more absurdly dangerous or age-inappropriate for children, and each is met with the same blank 'we don't have that.' The escalation culminates with candy cigarettes being 'discontinued because cigarettes are illegal.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation structure — each item is funnier than the last, with the switchblade-that-becomes-a-comb being a particularly inspired piece of nostalgia. The employee's deadpan responses ('I don't know what that is,' 'I don't think we have those') are perfectly pitched. The employee's wrong reason for candy cigarettes ('because cigarettes are illegal') is a funny capper on the escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You can do whatever the fuck you want.

jokes.text: "Oh, my God, a-a box of Nerds, nerd. Now, Nerds." — followed by employee producing Nerds, Frank staring at the tiny box in disbelief.
jokes.setup: Frank has been denied every nostalgic dangerous item. He asks for the most basic candy possible.
jokes.punchline: He gets Nerds — the one thing they DO have — but his reaction suggests even this is a profound disappointment. The 'nerd, nerd' callback on the word is an incidental wordplay bonus.
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke — after Frank's escalating demands, the fact that the only thing they have is Nerds (which aren't even dangerous) is a satisfying punchline to the sequence. The 'nerd, nerd' echo is accidental wordplay but adds a fun texture.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: 'Cause you're a jerk.

jokes.text: "What is, what is this? Where's the mouse hall? ... So you're telling me they shut down the Ride to Kid City for a superstore?"
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis discover major renovations have been made to Risk E. Rat's.
jokes.punchline: The beloved childhood feature has been replaced with a mundane superstore, triggering genuine grief in two grown men.
jokes.explanation: Functional observational humor about childhood nostalgia being ruined. Gets the job done as scene-setting but isn't a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: They used to put 'em on the waitresses without them knowing it... because then you could cop a feel and they couldn't say anything because if they did, they'd lose their jobs.

jokes.text: "Risk E. does not wear a helmet, remember? If he would fall and hit his head, he would say... 'That's what the bone's for.'"
jokes.setup: The updated Risk E. mascot now wears a safety helmet, which Mac and Dennis find offensive.
jokes.punchline: Their fond memory of Risk E. is that he would demonstrate that helmet-wearing is unnecessary by cracking kids on the back of the head. His catchphrase was 'That's what the bone is for.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best gags. 'That's what the bone is for!' as a children's mascot catchphrase about skull durability, delivered as the rat hits children in the head, is inspired dark comedy. The specificity of the catchphrase and the physical business together create a brilliantly wrong piece of fictional nostalgia. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — sharp, unexpected, quotable, and character-revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No, it was the '50s. It was fine.

jokes.text: "Yeah, yeah. It's great for the boys. And it's also good for the girls because then they know what they're supposed to look like. It's aspirational."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are defending the existence of sexy animatronic breasts at a children's restaurant as educational for boys.
jokes.punchline: Dennis extends the logic: it's also educational for girls — it tells them what their bodies 'should' look like. This is delivered as a sincere, positive framing.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis. His pseudo-intellectual reframing of objectification as 'aspirational' for women is perfectly in character for a man with serious narcissistic/misogynist tendencies. The word 'aspirational' is doing a lot of comedic heavy lifting here.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are they hot, dork? Are you trying to tell me that these sticks of molten cheese that just came out of the deep fryer, they're hot?

jokes.text: "I feel like Risk E.'s walled off in there, and I think Risk E. would want us to take a risk right now. He would want us to do it. Do it, whatever we want."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are frustrated that the backstage is inaccessible.
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes the spirit of Risk E. Rat as a philosophical justification for breaking and entering — using the brand's 'do whatever you want' message as a sincere permission slip for adult men to trespass into a children's entertainment venue.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-use of the episode's theme — the gang's self-justification for bad behavior is especially funny when the justification is a rat mascot's catchphrase. Ties the theme of the episode together.

dialogue.speaker: Dapper Duck
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't stutter. I have delightful diction.

jokes.text: "These balls have no weight to 'em. Back in my day, you could crush a man's skull with one of these."
jokes.setup: Frank is playing Skee-Ball at the newly renovated Risk E. Rat's.
jokes.punchline: Frank's complaint about the lighter Skee-Ball is that it's no longer capable of lethal head trauma, which he remembers fondly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. The gap between 'Skee-Ball' and 'crush a man's skull' is enormous, the delivery is completely deadpan, and it arrives mid-scene without buildup. Frank's violent nostalgia hits its peak here. At the 8.0 anchor level — sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, economical. 'Back in my day, you could crush a man's skull with one of these' is a great standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You d-d-d-d-d-do-do st-st-st-st-stutter.

jokes.text: Mac approaches a child at the Skee-Ball machine and immediately starts competing with and then berating him.
jokes.setup: Mac discovers a kid who is good at Skee-Ball and has 7,000 tickets.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being impressed or nice, Mac immediately brags ('I got 7,000, better than you') and then commands the child not to get his mom.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny dynamic — the gang bullying children and acting worse than them. Mac being competitive with a small child is in character, though the execution doesn't have a standout line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You were the retard.

jokes.text: "Yeah, you can. This is America. You can do whatever the fuck you want." — to a child, about pooling tickets.
jokes.setup: The child tells Mac you're not allowed to pool tickets.
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes American freedom and immediately swears at a child in a kids' restaurant, as if 'this is America' is both a legal argument and a parenting philosophy.
jokes.explanation: Good gag — the 'this is America' rhetoric deployed to justify pooling Skee-Ball tickets is a nice absurdist scale mismatch. The casual 'whatever the fuck you want' to a child lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, he's a duck. I wouldn't say that about a human.

jokes.text: "You can eat as much candy as you want. You're at Risk E. Rat's. That's the whole point. You can do whatever you want." — "I want my mom." — "You're not getting your mom!"
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to liberate the child from parental constraints, telling him he can eat whatever he wants.
jokes.punchline: The child's simple response — 'I want my mom' — reveals he's not being liberated, he's frightened, and Mac's refusal to let him have his mom is the horror of the scene.
jokes.explanation: "You're not getting your mom!" is a great punchline — it's delivered by Mac as a continuation of his 'freedom' philosophy but reads as genuinely threatening. The escalation from candy to maternal separation is a good darkening of the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Was he supposed to be Black?

jokes.text: Mac and child are sent to the 'Time-Out Room' — but it's now the 'Feelings Center.'
jokes.setup: Earlier Mac fondly described the Time-Out Room. Now he ends up in it.
jokes.punchline: The room has been renamed the 'Feelings Center' — a perfect update of the same concept into therapeutic language Mac will find humiliating.
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure — Mac longed for old-school punishment involving shame and head trauma, and instead gets a Feelings Center with a talking dog therapist. The gap between what he wanted and what he got is the joke. Rewatch bonus because knowing the callback makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: They should have monster voices because we need monster representation.

jokes.text: "You know, it was just so much cooler when they were like little plastic pieces of cheese with the joke on 'em. You'd read the joke and toss it in the trash."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are using new electronic scanners for the joke hunt.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's preferred version of the joke hunt involved literally throwing away the jokes after reading them — the experience, not the content, was the point.
jokes.explanation: Mild observational joke. Functional but not a standout. The 'toss it in the trash' detail is a nice specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This could be science is what you're saying... This is for the good of... future robots, right?

jokes.text: "You know what they used to do? They used to put 'em on the waitresses without them knowing it. Yeah, that was the fun thing, because then you could cop a feel and they couldn't say anything because if they did, they'd lose their jobs."
jokes.setup: Dennis is wistfully describing the old-school version of the cheese-hunt game.
jokes.punchline: His fond memory of the game is that it was a system for institutionalized sexual harassment of waitstaff with professional coercion baked in.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis. His nostalgia for systems that enabled predatory behavior is exactly on-brand, delivered as innocent memory. The specificity of the institutional coercion ('they couldn't say anything because if they did, they'd lose their jobs') makes this darkly precise rather than just offensive for shock value. Charlie's 'that's terrible' / Dennis's 'no, it was the '50s, it was fine' is a perfect beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: They-they took her tits off. They literally sanded 'em off!

jokes.text: "That's terrible." / "No, it was the '50s. It was fine."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just described a system of institutionalized sexual harassment as a fun game.
jokes.punchline: Charlie, who is himself a terrible person, calls this terrible — and Dennis dismisses it with the era as justification.
jokes.explanation: The two-beat exchange is tight and funny. Charlie being the moral voice of the scene is ironic given his own behavior throughout the series. 'No, it was the '50s, it was fine' is a quotable piece of historical dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This is a sad day for women's rights.

jokes.text: "Are they hot, dork? Are you trying to tell me that these sticks of molten cheese that just came out of the deep fryer, they're hot?"
jokes.setup: A server brings mozzarella sticks and says 'please be careful, they're hot.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis launches into a sarcastic takedown of the server for stating the obvious, calling him a 'dork' and walking through the entire self-evident logic.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis sarcasm — the disproportionate cruelty toward service staff over trivial matters is a consistent Dennis character note. The 'sticks of molten cheese' construction is funny. Not an exceptional joke but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You are stupid. It's 'cause you're stupid.

jokes.text: "Thank you so much for helping me out. What'd I've done if you weren't here? Bye. Beat it. Bye, Jesse."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just publicly humiliated the server about the hot food warning.
jokes.punchline: He dismisses him with a fake thank-you that becomes increasingly contemptuous, ending by calling him by name in a dismissive 'shoo' tone.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous beat. 'Bye, Jesse' is a funny specific touch — using the server's name as a dismissal is somehow worse than not knowing it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You got no freedom, which means you got no balls... you're never gonna hate yourself enough to stop being bad and grow some balls.

jokes.text: "Hey there, Dingbat Duck." / "Actually, it's Dapper Duck now." / "How do you like the delectable duds?"
jokes.setup: An updated mascot character greets Dennis and Charlie at the table.
jokes.punchline: The mascot has been rebranded — same character, now alliteratively polished. The 'delectable duds' line is the mascot trying to be charming.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the more elaborate stutter gag that follows. Functional but the main comedy comes from the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It gets jalapeño business... You got to do it with an accent. It gets 'all-up-in-yo' business.

jokes.text: Mac insists on calling Dapper Duck 'Dingbat Duck' and demands to know where his stutter went
jokes.setup: Dapper Duck mascot greets them and introduces himself with the new name
jokes.punchline: Mac refuses the rebrand and demands the stutter back, then demonstrates by stuttering at the mascot
jokes.explanation: Mac demanding the mascot reclaim his disability for comedy purposes is a solid cringe beat. The mascot's patient 'I have delightful diction' versus Mac's 'you d-d-d-do stutter' is a nice back-and-forth.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: But I got to know who the victim is in order for me to laugh at them.

jokes.text: "You were the retard." / "Whoa, whoa." / "What? Don't say... come on." / "Well, he's a duck. I wouldn't say that about a human. But you're telling me I can't say a duck is retarded?"
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to describe what made Dingbat Duck funny.
jokes.punchline: He uses a slur and then, when corrected, makes the tortured argument that the word is acceptable for ducks but not humans — genuinely trying to work out the logic of his own position.
jokes.explanation: Very good character moment for Charlie — he isn't malicious, he's genuinely trying to work out the logic of why the word would be acceptable in this context, and his reasoning ('he's a duck') is both wrong and completely sincere. The specificity of the duck/human distinction is funny because Charlie believes he's being nuanced.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, there is no bar.

jokes.text: "Suppose he walked up here, and his feet were on backwards and his beak was on the inside of his head, what, then I could call him retarded?" / "Well, no. Then you're dealing with a mutant duck, and that's not funny."
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to identify at what point a duck's disability would justify using the slur.
jokes.punchline: He constructs a hypothetical mutant duck with backwards feet and an internal beak, and Dennis's correction isn't 'that's offensive' but 'a mutant duck isn't funny.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. Charlie constructing a grotesque mutant duck anatomy ('feet on backwards, beak on the inside of his head') as a philosophical threshold test is brilliantly absurd. Dennis's response — correcting the COMEDY of the scenario rather than the morality — is perfect character writing for both. 'A mutant duck, and that's not funny' as a moral position is a great inversion.

dialogue.line: Did he just say Robbie-pizza.com?

jokes.text: "His mouth was retarded." / "Stop saying 'retarded.'"
jokes.setup: Charlie is continuing to try to find a way to use the word he wants.
jokes.punchline: His compromise is to apply the word specifically to the duck's mouth rather than the whole duck — as if this solves the problem.
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper to the word debate. Charlie's solution — apply it to a body part rather than the whole creature — is exactly the kind of wrong-headed logic he'd use. 'Stop saying retarded' as the flat punchline is very funny in its exhausted delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You cannot call a place a website.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover the entire animatronic band dismantled and stored in a back room.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis went backstage hoping to find Justine the Teen Dream.
jokes.punchline: Instead of one topless robot, they find the entire Animatronic No Rules Band in pieces in storage — including Spaz the drummer, Chef Greaseball Linguini, and Dr. Slice the Funky Funkosapien.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag with great character names — 'Spaz the drummer,' 'Chef Greaseball Linguini,' and 'Dr. Slice the Funky Funkosapien' are a highlight of the episode's world-building. Each name is a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We recreate the old Risk E.'s so that these kids can have the same experience that we had when we were younger

jokes.text: "Was he supposed to be Black?" regarding the purple animatronic character Dr. Slice.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are examining the dismantled band members.
jokes.punchline: Dennis asks if the purple monster was 'supposed to be Black,' and after some hedging they confirm: yes, it was a white guy doing a Black voice in a purple costume.
jokes.explanation: Smart satirical comedy about how racial representation in entertainment used to work. The 'purple so it's not racist' logic is a recognizable real-world phenomenon that the show correctly identifies as the same thing. Mac's growing discomfort is good character work.

dialogue.line: Where's my son?! Where's my son?!

jokes.text: "But they are purple. Monsters. You know, like, monsters are purple. Blue, green, purple, orange, and we can't just not have purple monsters in bands anymore."
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining why a white guy doing a Black voice in a purple costume is problematic.
jokes.punchline: Mac's argument for monster representation — that purple monsters exist and deserve band membership — is simultaneously absurd, sincere, and accidentally a better argument than what they were actually debating.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier moments in the episode's race-commentary section. Mac pivoting to monster representation is a genuinely good satirical move — it derails the conversation into something absurd while still being logically coherent within the fiction. 'Monster representation' is a funny concept.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They weren't prepared for that amount of fun.

jokes.text: "They should have monster voices. Because we need monster representation. So we can't just put them in boxes."
jokes.setup: Mac has committed to the monster representation argument.
jokes.punchline: He extends the logic: monsters deserve authentic voice representation in entertainment, and stereotyping monsters into generic voices is a form of pigeonholing.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. 'We can't put them in boxes' applied to fictional purple monsters is a solid piece of satirical writing about how identity politics discourse can be extended absurdly.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ah, they won't find me.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis find Justine's torso in storage and are genuinely moved: 'Oh, no. Sweet Justine. What have they done to you?'
jokes.setup: They've been searching the whole episode for the animatronic
jokes.punchline: Their reaction to finding her disassembled torso is genuine grief — treating a robot mannequin with the reverence of discovering a fallen friend
jokes.explanation: 'Sweet Justine. What have they done to you?' treating an animatronic torso like a war casualty is good character comedy. The sincerity is what sells it.

jokes.text: Mac finds Justine's torso — and reveals the animatronic breasts are still there and highly detailed.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been searching for Justine in the storage room.
jokes.punchline: Mac finds her disassembled torso and reports with increasing enthusiasm: 'Very accurate design. Nipples. All the curves.'
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the Justine setup. Mac's itemized inventory of the robot's anatomical features ('Interesting... Nipples... Fascinating... Wow, good') delivered as a scientist examining a specimen is funny.

jokes.text: "We could just be two mature men with an interest in robotics. This could be science." / "I think this is a scientific experiment."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are still deliberating over whether undressing the robot is okay.
jokes.punchline: They reframe two adult men undressing a robot torso in a storage closet as scientific inquiry.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the rationalization sequence. The gang's ability to retroactively justify any behavior through invented framing is one of the show's consistent themes, and 'this is for the good of science' applied to robot nudity is funny.

jokes.text: Mac removes the shirt to reveal the breasts have been sanded off — just a flat, smooth surface where they were.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have built up to undressing Justine as the culmination of their entire plan.
jokes.punchline: The breasts have been physically removed — 'sanded off' — leaving a smooth surface. The visual reveal undercuts the entire buildup.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the whole first act has been building to this reveal, and the payoff is a complete deflation. The fact that someone physically 'sanded off' the robot's breasts is a great absurdist image. This is the climax of the episode's A-plot and it delivers.

jokes.text: "They-they took her tits off. They literally sanded 'em off! They mutilated this poor woman."
jokes.setup: Mac has discovered the robot's breasts have been removed.
jokes.punchline: He frames this as mutilation of 'this poor woman' — applying concern for a robot's bodily autonomy that he would never extend to actual women.
jokes.explanation: Very good character work — Mac referring to the robot as 'this poor woman' and framing the modification as 'mutilation' shows how thoroughly he has projected humanity onto the robot while remaining blind to actual women's autonomy throughout the episode.

jokes.text: "Goddamn libs." / "And this could be the religious conservatives, too. You know, you don't know. / That's true. / Lopping tits off feels like a, feels like a religious move."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to figure out who is responsible for removing the robot's breasts.
jokes.punchline: They cover both political extremes — liberals and religious conservatives — as potential culprits for animatronic robot breast removal, arriving at the bipartisan conclusion that everyone is crazy.
jokes.explanation: Smart political comedy that the show does well — Mac's reflexive 'goddamn libs' followed by Dennis's equally plausible 'could be religious conservatives' creates a both-sides absurdism. 'Lopping tits off feels like a religious move' is a great line.

jokes.text: "This is a sad day for women's rights."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are mourning the removal of the animatronic breasts.
jokes.punchline: Mac invokes women's rights — a concept he has shown zero genuine interest in — to frame his disappointment about not seeing a robot's chest as a feminist issue.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The gap between Mac's actual behavior toward women throughout the episode and his invocation of 'women's rights' to describe his disappointment at not seeing robot breasts is perfectly constructed irony. It's short, it's character-specific, it lands as the button on the entire scene, and it's deeply quotable. Mac's hypocrisy is exposed in six words. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — sharp, economical, character-specific, quotable.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis are in the 'Feelings Center' with a talking-dog therapist conducting an emotion circle.
jokes.setup: Mac was sent to the Time-Out Room for scaring a child. The modern Time-Out Room is now the Feelings Center.
jokes.punchline: It's a formal therapy circle, run by what appears to be a costumed talking dog therapist, treating Mac and Sam the same way — as emotional equals who need to process feelings.
jokes.explanation: Great payoff to the episode's theme — the contrast between Mac's ideal punishment (shame-based head trauma) and the actual modern Feelings Center is perfect. The talking dog therapist treating a grown man and a child the same way is funny.

jokes.text: "Well, I... feel angry. / Is there anything else? / Yeah, I feel... misunderstood. / Unheard."
jokes.setup: The dog therapist asks Mac how he's feeling.
jokes.punchline: Mac's feelings — angry, misunderstood, unheard — are delivered with genuine sincerity, but they're accurate descriptions of Mac's whole existence, applied here to not seeing robot breasts.
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Mac being angry, misunderstood, and unheard is a surprisingly accurate description of his permanent emotional state. The therapy setting makes it funnier because a dog is extracting genuine therapeutic content from a man who is there for the wrong reasons.

jokes.text: Mac's emotional check-in: 'I feel angry... misunderstood... unheard.'
jokes.setup: The dog therapist asks how Mac is feeling
jokes.punchline: Mac, despite his loud objection to the Feelings Center, accurately names his emotions — revealing the irony that he actually needs therapy
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap: Mac is raging about not wanting to be in a feelings center, but his answers — 'angry, misunderstood, unheard' — are textbook therapy responses that suggest he's been in therapy (or needs it badly). The irony that the worst possible person for this program is nailing it is good character work.

jokes.text: "You are stupid. It's 'cause you're stupid." — to a child, by Mac.
jokes.setup: Sam the child says he feels stupid talking about his feelings.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately confirms this is accurate, telling the child he IS stupid and that's why.
jokes.explanation: Good mean-spirited gag. The economy is great — Mac not missing a beat to agree that the child is stupid is very funny. The dog's 'Mac' interruption implies it was said quickly enough that the dog barely had time to react.

jokes.text: Mac and Dog get increasingly stuck on whether Sam is being 'sassy,' with 'sassy' escalating into the dominant word of the therapy session.
jokes.setup: Mac calls Sam sassy. The dog therapist tries to redirect, but the word 'sassy' takes over the entire conversation.
jokes.punchline: The sassy debate escalates to 'I'm mired in the sass' — a grown man in a children's therapy circle has become consumed by one descriptor applied to an eight-year-old.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm mired in the sass' is a genuinely funny line — the word 'mired' applied to 'sass' is an unexpected collision of registers. The escalating repetition of 'sassy' in a therapy context is good sustained comedy.

jokes.text: "That's not the point of Risk E. Rat's." — from an eight-year-old, in therapy.
jokes.setup: Sam says he doesn't want to be in the Feelings Center.
jokes.punchline: The child is making the exact same argument as Mac and the gang — that this isn't what Risk E. Rat's is for — which puts him in unwilling alignment with the people terrorizing him.
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the child and his abuser are on the same side philosophically. This creates a brief moment where Mac and Sam bond over shared contempt for the Feelings Center.

jokes.text: "You're a talking dog. I'm out of here."
jokes.setup: The dog therapist says 'there's no shame in making a mistake.' Mac argues there IS shame, it's how you learn. Dog says 'Hey, I'm a licensed psychotherapist.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's rebuttal to the dog's credential is simply: you are a dog. I'm leaving.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. Mac has been engaging with the dog's therapy on its own terms for the entire scene, and his exit is simply the acknowledgment that it's a dog. The timing — after several minutes of genuine engagement — makes the deflation huge. 'You're a talking dog. I'm out of here.' is a highly quotable line, delivered as the most reasonable thing Mac has said all episode.

jokes.text: "If you're not held accountable, you feel no guilt. If you feel no guilt, you feel no shame. If you got no shame... you're never gonna hate yourself enough to stop being bad and grow some balls."
jokes.setup: Mac is delivering his philosophy of discipline to Sam the child.
jokes.punchline: Mac's entire ethical framework — that guilt, shame, and self-hatred are the correct path to moral growth, culminating in 'grow some balls' — is delivered as sincere parenting advice to a small child.
jokes.explanation: One of the best character monologues in the episode. Mac's self-loathing-based ethical system is perfectly distilled here — his entire philosophy of human development is rooted in shame as the primary motivator. That this is delivered to a child as sincere advice, and that it's also a perfect description of Mac's own psychological damage, makes it a great piece of character writing. The escalating chain logic ('if A then B, if B then C') gives it a rhetorical structure that's both funny and reveals Mac's genuinely warped worldview.

jokes.text: "You diddle this kid, you're definitely on camera. I don't know if you want to be alone with him."
jokes.setup: Mac is in the Feelings Center with the child. Dennis appears to have come to check on him.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's concern isn't about Mac's behavior or the child's wellbeing — it's a practical warning that potential abuse would be filmed.
jokes.explanation: Very dark and very Dennis. His warning to Mac is entirely about optics and evidence, not morality. 'You diddle this kid, you're definitely on camera' is a genuinely disturbing line delivered as practical advice between friends — which is exactly the kind of dark humor Always Sunny excels at. The casualness of 'I don't know if you want to be alone with him' as the follow-up is what makes it land.

jokes.text: "What does a nosy pepper do? It gets jalapeño business." Dennis and Charlie argue about what ethnicity the punchline is mocking.
jokes.setup: Charlie finds the last piece of cheese for the joke hunt. The joke is printed on it.
jokes.punchline: The jalapeño pun itself is functional, but the meta-argument about whose accent the punchline requires, and therefore who is the 'victim,' is the real joke.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-comedy about joke structure. The jalapeño pun is old but the deconstruction of it — 'you've got to put some sass on it,' 'I need to know who the victim is to laugh' — is sharp and reveals how the gang actually thinks about humor.

jokes.text: "I got to know who the victim is in order for me to laugh at them."
jokes.setup: Charlie doesn't find the jalapeño pun funny until he knows whose expense the joke is at.
jokes.punchline: He articulates the actual logic of a certain type of comedy — you need a target — but delivers it as if it's a reasonable, respectable requirement for a joke to work.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-comedic line. Charlie accidentally articulating the mechanics of punchdown comedy as if they're a virtue — 'I need to know who the victim is' — is both a character joke and a surprisingly sharp piece of comedy commentary. Very quotable.

jokes.text: "In this scenario it's whites because white people are the only people who don't have the accent to pull off the joke." / "Well, that's racist." / "That is racist, and I don't appreciate it."
jokes.setup: Dennis has figured out who the 'victim' of the jalapeño pun is.
jokes.punchline: Both Dennis and Charlie immediately declare this racist — but only because they are white and are the target, not out of any principled opposition to racism.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest satirical moments. After an extended episode of casually racist observations and defenses, the moment a joke targets white people, Dennis and Charlie immediately declare it racist. The hypocrisy is perfectly constructed and the delivery is tight. 'That is racist, and I don't appreciate it' from two men who have spent the episode casually deploying every form of prejudice is the episode's most precise satire.

jokes.text: "I don't 100% understand what satire means."
jokes.setup: Charlie says this after an argument about whether the cheese hunt jokes are satire.
jokes.punchline: Charlie, who has been unknowingly performing satire about racism for the entire episode, admits he doesn't know what satire is.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely good meta-line. The show itself is satire, the episode is satire, and the character who is the instrument of that satire admits he doesn't know what satire means. It's also just very Charlie — honest, oblivious, and delivered flat.

jokes.text: "Guys, I hate to admit it, but this place sucks."
jokes.setup: The gang has had a terrible time at the renovated Risk E. Rat's.
jokes.punchline: Mac has to 'admit' this despite overwhelming evidence — the missing bar, the sanded robot, the Feelings Center — suggesting he held on to hope longer than he should have.
jokes.explanation: Functional transition joke. The 'I hate to admit it' framing is funny given everything they've experienced, but it's not a standout moment.

jokes.text: "Like, who are the weirdos with the kids?" / "I think it's their parents." / "The parents should be in the bar." / "Charlie, there is no bar." / "What? Are you serious? They got rid of the bar?"
jokes.setup: The gang notices that parents are present in the main space rather than in a bar.
jokes.punchline: Charlie can't process the concept of a children's restaurant without a soundproofed bar for parents to get drunk in — and refers to the parents supervising their own children as 'weirdos.'
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the bar established in the opening scene. 'Who are the weirdos with the kids?' applied to parents is a funny inversion. Charlie's disbelief at the bar's removal is well-played.

jokes.text: "Did he just say Robbie-pizza.com? / Did they change the name? / You cannot call a place a website. That's crazy. / He's not Risk E. anymore? He's Robbie now?"
jokes.setup: The animatronic show begins, and the mascot sings 'rocking out at Robbie-pizza.com'
jokes.punchline: The beloved childhood mascot has been rebranded as a website URL — the ultimate symbol of corporate modernization destroying something sacred.
jokes.explanation: 'You cannot call a place a website' is a good, specific observational line. The genuine grief at 'He's not Risk E. anymore? He's Robbie now?' is funny because it's completely sincere disappointment.

jokes.text: "We recreate the old Risk E.'s so that these kids can have the same experience that we had when we were younger and they can perhaps tell the tale."
jokes.setup: The gang decides to intervene in the show and restore the 'real' Risk E. Rat's experience.
jokes.punchline: 'They can perhaps tell the tale' — Dennis accidentally implies the experience may be survival-level dangerous.
jokes.explanation: 'They can perhaps tell the tale' is a funny sinister slip — Dennis frames giving children a fun time as something they may or may not survive. Very Dennis.

jokes.text: "Fun!" — followed immediately by screaming, chaos, and a parent yelling 'Where's my son?!'
jokes.setup: The gang has set up their version of the 'real' Risk E. Rat's experience. Frank is about to 'throw the switch.'
jokes.punchline: The immediate cut from 'Fun!' to screaming chaos and a panicked parent yelling 'Where's my son?!' — the gang's version of fun is apparently terrifying.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The cut from 'Fun!' — the single word summarizing everything they set up — to immediate screaming and parental panic is a perfect comedic payoff to the entire episode's escalation. The 'Where's my son?!' is the perfect specific detail. Classic Sunny ending structure: the gang's plan causes disaster, they briefly reflect, and immediately think about escaping liability. Comparable to the best scene-enders in the series. High impact because the anticipation has built for the whole act.

jokes.text: "Well, that got out of hand." / "Yeah. Yeah, these kids, they just, they weren't prepared for that amount of fun."
jokes.setup: The gang's recreation of old Risk E. Rat's has caused panic and trauma.
jokes.punchline: Their post-mortem is delivered with complete calm — the problem wasn't what they did, it was that the children weren't ready for 'that amount of fun.'
jokes.explanation: 'They weren't prepared for that amount of fun' is a good line — it reframes trauma as the kids being underprepared, which is the gang's standard deflection from accountability. Classic Sunny post-disaster rationalization.

jokes.text: "That's because they were sheltered too much. / Right. / I'm glad that they signed the waiver, though."
jokes.setup: The gang is rationalizing the chaos they caused.
jokes.punchline: Frank brings up the waiver — a callback to the opening scene — as the silver lining. The waiver they coerced kids' parents into signing now protects the gang from legal liability.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the waiver from the opening — it was established as a minor inconvenience and returns as the gang's legal protection. The payoff is satisfying. The structure of the whole episode's cold open detail paying off at the end is solid writing.

jokes.text: "Although you didn't, you didn't sign anything." / "Ah, they won't find me."
jokes.setup: Mac is glad about the waiver. Dennis notes Frank didn't sign it.
jokes.punchline: Frank's response — 'Ah, they won't find me' — treats legal liability as a game of hide and seek that Frank is confident he can win.
jokes.explanation: 'Ah, they won't find me' is a great Frank line — maximum confidence, minimum self-awareness. Frank's approach to legal jeopardy is exactly this breezy. The economy is excellent.

tmdb_overview: The gang goes to Risk E. Rat's, finding it updated with safety and overcautiousness. Dee takes Frank on a scavenger hunt to find risqué jokes hidden throughout the establishment. Mac plays Skee-Ball to win tickets for a prize.
